title: Leya – the latest addition to MSA Innovation Lab
author: Mannheimer Swartling

dom.t: Legora partnerships: Adoption needs selected workflows and training

mo.t: Legal platforms: Content and governance differentiate workflows
Legora expansion: Workflow usefulness must sustain global scale
Legora partnerships: Adoption needs selected workflows and training

kp.k: Generative AI targets repetitive work to refocus lawyers
kp.d: The announcement describes Leya as a generative AI platform intended to streamline repetitive and manual legal tasks so lawyers can concentrate on advanced legal and strategic matters. This is a stated design purpose and anticipated change in lawyers’ work, rather than a measured productivity finding.
qs: Leya’s platform is designed to efficientise and optimise repetitive and manual tasks in the legal sector.

By streamlining and simplifying significant portions of the legal work, the platform  enables law firms and legal professionals to work more efficiently and focus on the more advanced legal and strategic matters.

kp.k: Compliance and privacy qualify the vendor’s automation ambition
kp.d: Leya CEO Max Junestrand frames assistance with all repetitive and manual tasks as an ambition, explicitly conditioned on not compromising compliance or privacy. The statement does not describe safeguards or provide evidence of their effectiveness.
qs: Our ambition with Leya is that the platform will help with all the repetitive and manual tasks so that lawyers instead can focus on the advanced key issues. Of course without compromising with compliance or privacy, says Max Junestrand, CEO at Leya.

kp.k: Collaboration seeks workflow, quality and client-experience improvements
kp.d: Mannheimer Swartling presents its partnership with Leya as part of ongoing innovation intended to improve lawyers’ workflows and legal advice. It lists accuracy, quality and customer experience among collaboration highlights, without reporting quantified outcomes or an evaluation.
qs: The partnership between Mannheimer Swartling and Leya is another major step for the firm’s ongoing innovation efforts, with the purpose to improve the lawyers’ workflows and even further elevate the quality of our legal advice.

kp.k: Firm leadership treats AI adoption as strategic positioning
kp.d: Managing Partner Jan Dernestam links Leya’s approach to the firm’s ambition to lead in using AI in legal advice. He acknowledges potential disruption but endorses adoption, expressing confidence that incubator companies and collaborations will support that goal. These are leadership expectations, not demonstrated competitive outcomes.
qs: Leya’s approach is also completely in line with the firm’s goal to be the leading law firm when it comes to using AI in our legal advice.

AI may be disruptive, but just as with all our digital development during the recent years we embrace the immense leap that AI represents, and we are very much looking forward to our new co-opearation with Leya.
We are convinced that Leya together with our other incubator companies and collaborations will help us reach our, to say the least, ambitious goal, Jan Dernestam continues.

kp.k: Incubator connects legal expertise with technology development
kp.d: The announcement reports Leya’s admission to the firm’s legal-tech incubator and describes the incubator as a mechanism for sharing firm knowledge with businesses considered capable of transforming the legal industry. Its stated purposes combine support for entrepreneurs with streamlining and digitalising the firm’s workflows.
qs: Leya is a generative AI platform for the legal sector and the latest company to join our legal tech incubator.

In order to support entrepreneurs and innovators, and at the same time streamline and digitalise all of Mannheimer Swartling’s workflows, MSA Innovation Lab houses for instance a legal tech incubator.
Within the incubator we share all of our knowledge and experience with new businesses that we consider to have the potential to transform the legal industry.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Mannheimer Swartling presents Leya as a means of streamlining routine legal work, freeing lawyers for advanced legal and strategic matters, and improving service quality.
pts.d: The firm's announcement claims that Leya simplifies significant portions of legal work and enables greater efficiency. It identifies streamlined workflows, enhanced accuracy and quality, and improved customer experience as intended benefits of the collaboration. Leya CEO Max Junestrand describes helping with all repetitive and manual tasks as an ambition, allowing lawyers to concentrate on advanced key issues. These are claims about augmenting lawyers and reallocating their attention, not explicit predictions of job losses or autonomous replacement. Managing Partner Jan Dernestam characterises AI as potentially disruptive and expresses confidence that Leya and the firm's other collaborations will help it become a leading law firm in using AI in legal advice.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The announcement relies on product descriptions and leadership assessments rather than reported measurements of results.
pts.d: No productivity data, accuracy benchmarks, client outcomes, named task demonstrations, or implementation case results are supplied. Junestrand states the product's ambition, while Dernestam offers a favourable comparative assessment without describing its method or comparison set. Leya's admission to the firm's incubator and acceptance to Y Combinator provide institutional context, but the announcement does not present them as measured evidence of efficiency or quality improvements.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2023 announcement combines present-tense capability claims with prospective collaboration goals, without a delivery deadline.
pts.d: The firm's narrative says the platform already enables efficiency, but the quoted speakers describe a platform under development and benefits they hope the new collaboration will achieve. No schedule, adoption threshold, or quantified target is stated. Junestrand explicitly qualifies the ambition to assist with routine work by saying compliance and privacy must not be compromised; the source does not explain how those safeguards will be achieved. Dernestam's prediction of leadership in AI-enabled advice is conditional on the contribution of Leya alongside other incubator companies and collaborations, rather than Leya alone.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The proposed benefits concern law firms and legal professionals, particularly Mannheimer Swartling's lawyers, with indirect benefits for clients.
pts.d: Lawyers are expected to spend less effort on repetitive and manual work and more on advanced legal and strategic questions. Mannheimer Swartling expects better workflows, higher-quality advice, and a stronger position in AI adoption. Clients are identified indirectly through the promised improvement in customer experience and advice quality. The announcement also positions its incubator as supporting entrepreneurs whose businesses may transform the legal industry. It does not specify effects on headcount, junior lawyers, billing, client prices, or access to justice. Leya is presented as a legal-technology platform company, not as an alternative legal service provider delivering legal work.
